Three public-domain stories fit the lights-out hour: Saki's 'The Open Window' (about 8 minutes) for 8–12s, E. F. Benson's 'The Bus-Conductor' (about 23) for teens and his 'How Fear Departed from the Long Gallery' (about 39) for adults.
The AASM recommends 9–12 hours of sleep at ages 6–12 and 8–10 at 13–18; lights out at 10:30 pm and up at 8 am gives a 10-year-old 9.5 hours.
Settle six things in the parents' group chat three days ahead, from allergies and two emergency numbers to film ratings and phone rules.
48.3% of pages shared through SubhSandesh are opened on a phone, so the plan gives phones a basket and a curfew rather than a ban.

faqs.question: What do you actually do at a Halloween sleepover?
faqs.answer: Run it as eight slots: arrival, dinner, one main activity, a film, a lights-out story hour, a midnight snack, breakfast and pickup. For 8–12s that means ghost-name badges, pizza bagels, pillowcase monsters, a U or PG film, Saki's 'The Open Window' and a fake midnight at 10:15 pm.

faqs.question: What time should a kids' Halloween sleepover start and finish?
faqs.answer: Our plan runs 6 pm to 10 am for ages 8–12, with lights out at 10:30 pm. Teens shift to 7 pm with an 11 am pickup, and adults run 7:30 pm to 11 am.

faqs.question: Which scary story can I read aloud to 10-year-olds at lights out?
faqs.answer: Saki's 'The Open Window' (1914) is 1,208 words, about 8 minutes at 150 words a minute, and its twist is that the ghost story was invented. Preview the last paragraph, which mentions a night in a newly dug grave.

faqs.question: Which ghost story works for teenagers once the lights are off?
faqs.answer: E. F. Benson's 'The Bus-Conductor' (1912) suits most 13–17s: about 3,462 words, roughly 23 minutes read aloud, with dread rather than gore. Name it in the parents' group chat first so any parent can veto it.

faqs.question: How scary should the movie be at a sleepover?
faqs.answer: Agree the title and rating in the parents' group chat before the night, never on it. For 8–12s pick one U or PG film under 95 minutes; for teens the strictest parent sets the rating cap and guests vote within it.

faqs.question: What should I ask other parents before hosting?
faqs.answer: Six things, three days ahead: allergies and where any auto-injector is kept, two emergency numbers per child, pickup time and driver, phone rules, film titles and ratings, and anything private such as bedwetting or night fears, sent to you alone.

faqs.question: What if a child wants to go home in the middle of the night?
faqs.answer: Move them to a quiet, lit room with a drink, offer 20 minutes with you or a call home, and if they choose home, ring the parent together on speaker. An AAP report by Thurber and Walton (2007) notes almost everyone feels some homesickness away from familiar people.

faqs.question: How much sleep do kids need after a sleepover night?
faqs.answer: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours for ages 6 to 12 and 8 to 10 for 13 to 18. Lights out at 10:30 pm with an 8 am wake-up gives a 10-year-old 9.5 hours; let teens sleep until about 9:30.

faqs.question: What do adults do at a grown-up Halloween sleepover?
faqs.answer: The same eight slots from 7:30 pm: a sleepover time capsule, a childhood-dinner revival, blind clay monsters, the film that scared you at 12, Benson's 'How Fear Departed from the Long Gallery' at midnight and a blind cereal tasting. Assign beds in the invitation and name an 11 am exit.

faqs.question: Is a sleepover a good idea for a child under 8?
faqs.answer: Often a 'late-over' works better: pyjamas, a film and the Saki story, then collection at 9 pm. A child with diagnosed anxiety or night fears should have their parent choose the story and film.

faqs.question: What can I send the friend who hosted the sleepover?
faqs.answer: Our /happy-halloween page in bestie mode ends with 'Will you be my boo-st friend forever?' and a 1080×1920 Boo License, with up to six of your photos and a letter read by torchlight. It is a one-person greeting, not a party tool, and its interface is English only.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Sleepover Ideas, Hour by Hour From Arrival to Pickup

The best Halloween sleepover ideas follow the clock: arrival, dinner, one main activity, a film, a lights-out story hour, a midnight snack, breakfast and pickup. Below are 25 ideas across those eight slots, each with an age band (8–12, 13–17 or adults), a time and materials, plus three public-domain stories timed for reading aloud.

We build greeting pages, not party kits, and two of our numbers shaped the phone rules. 48.3% of pages shared through SubhSandesh are opened on a phone, and 90.9% of started pages get finished and sent. Phones will be there anyway, so they get a basket and a curfew, not a ban.

Halloween is Saturday 31 October in 2026 and Sunday 31 October in 2027. In 2027, host on Saturday 30 October instead.

## What makes a Halloween sleepover different from a Halloween party?

A Halloween sleepover is an overnight stay at a friend's home lasting about 16 hours from a 6 pm arrival to a 10 am pickup. Unlike a party, it must end in sleep, so the scariest moment comes before a calming snack, never last.

A [2025 survey of 1,600 parents of children aged 1 to 17](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40522538) by Taranu and colleagues found 93% of children enjoyed at least one of 19 kinds of "recreational fear" activity, with distinct age trends. We read the abstract only; its lesson is to fit the fright to the age.

## 25 Halloween sleepover ideas, slot by slot from 6 pm to 10 am

Times are for a kids' night; the table gives teen and adult times. Each idea lists age band · time · materials.

### 1. Arrival, 6:00 pm: three icebreakers

- **Ghost-name badges** (8–12 · 15 min · card, markers): first initial plus birth month makes a spooky name, used until breakfast.
- **Sleeping-spot draw** (13–17 · 10 min · playing cards): highest card picks first; the joker sleeps nearest the door.
- **Sleepover time capsule** (adults · 20 min · one keepsake each): a childhood-sleepover photo or object, explained in two minutes.

### 2. Dinner, 6:30 pm: food guests assemble

- **Monster-mouth pizza bagels** (8–12 · 40 min · bagels, passata, cheese, olives, peppers): olive eyes, pepper fangs, an adult at the oven.
- **Mystery-bag quesadillas** (13–17 · 30 min · tortillas, five fillings in paper bags): pairs draw two bags blind. Check each bag against the allergy list.
- **Childhood-dinner revival** (adults · 45 min): the host cooks the childhood sleepover dinner that wins a group vote.

### 3. Main activity, 7:15 pm: one big make

- **Pillowcase monsters** (8–12 · 45 min · plain pillowcases, fabric markers): draw a face, sleep on it, take it home.
- **Tie-dye ghost tees** (13–17 · 45 min plus overnight · white tees, dye kit, zip bags): rinse at breakfast for a morning reveal.
- **Blind clay monsters** (adults · 60 min · air-dry clay): describe a monster for 30 seconds; your neighbour sculpts it unseen.

### 4. Movie, 8:15 pm: chosen in advance

- **Paper-ticket cinema** (8–12 · 100 min · drawn tickets, popcorn cones): one U or PG film under 95 minutes, agreed beforehand.
- **Rating-capped vote** (13–17 · about 2 hours · three-film shortlist): the strictest parent sets the cap; guests vote within it.
- **The film that scared you at 12** (adults · about 2 hours · paper slips): everyone nominates one, and you draw.

### 5. Lights out, 9:45 pm: the scary-story hour

A published story has a real ending; improvised ones drift into gore. All three are public domain; reading times use our estimated pace of 150 words a minute.

- **"The Open Window" by Saki, 1914** (8–12 · about 8 minutes, 1,208 words · one torch): a girl of fifteen invents a ghost story for a nervous visitor. From [Beasts and Super-Beasts](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/269); preview the last paragraph, which mentions a night in a fresh grave.
- **The "too much" ghost** (8–12 · all hour · paper ghosts, a jar): any child drops one in, no questions, and the reader skips to the twist.
- **"The Bus-Conductor" by E. F. Benson, 1912** (13–17 · about 23 minutes, 3,462 words · one torch): a hearse driver at dawn says "Just room for one inside, sir", and a month later a bus conductor wears his face. From [The Room in the Tower and Other Stories](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/72421).
- **"How Fear Departed from the Long Gallery" by E. F. Benson, 1912** (adults · about 39 minutes, 5,892 words · battery candle, two readers): a comic haunted-house tale with a grim backstory and a kind ending. Same book.

### 6. Midnight snack, 10:15 pm for kids, real midnight for teens

- **Fake midnight** (8–10 · 10 min · a clock set 1 hour 45 minutes fast, warm milk): it reads 12:00, and lights go out at 10:30.
- **Toastie at real midnight** (13–17 · 20 min · sandwich toaster, bread, cheese): nothing tastes better at 12:00 am.
- **Blind cereal tasting** (adults · 15 min · four childhood cereals): score them, then dispute the ranking.

### 7. Breakfast, 8:30 am: slow and warm

- **Squeeze-bottle bat pancakes** (8–12 · 30 min · batter bottle, non-stick pan): children draw the bat, an adult flips it.
- **Swamp smoothies and waffles** (13–17 · 20 min · spinach, banana, mango, waffles): rinse the tie-dye while the waffles toast.
- **Rank-the-night fry-up** (adults · 40 min): each guest presents one award, say loudest scream.

### 8. Pickup, 10:00 am: nothing left behind

- **Pack the pillowcase** (8–12 · 5 min): fold it with the ghost name inside so it reaches the right home.
- **Five-minute charger sweep** (13–17 · 5 min · a basket): cables, socks and hoodies in before the first car.
- **Ghost note for the host** (adults · 5 min · sticky notes): hide a thank-you note for them to find next week.

## Halloween sleepover timeline for kids, teens and adults

Eight slots, grouped into four blocks, with start times per age band.

| Timeline slot | Kids 8–12 | Teens 13–17 | Adults |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arrival and dinner | 6:00 pm · ghost names, bagels | 7:00 pm · spot draw, quesadillas | 7:30 pm · time capsule, childhood dinner |
| Main activity and movie | 7:15 pm · pillowcases, PG film | 8:15 pm · tie-dye, capped film | 9:00 pm · clay, childhood scare film |
| Story hour and snack | 9:45 pm · Saki, 8 min; fake midnight | 11:15 pm · Benson, 23 min; toastie | 12:00 am · Benson, 39 min; cereal |
| Sleep to pickup | Lights out 10:30; pickup 10:00 | Lights out 12:45; pickup 11:00 | Leave 11:00 |

The kids' column protects 9.5 hours of sleep and the teens' about 8.75, both inside the ranges below.

## The host-parent group chat: 6 things to settle 3 days ahead

Message every family three days before and ask each to reply. Vague answers become 11 pm calls.

- **Allergies:** every allergen and where any auto-injector is kept.
- **Emergency numbers:** two per child, plus your address and mobile.
- **Pickup:** 10 am for kids, 11 am for teens, and which adult collects.
- **Phones:** into a basket at lights out, back at breakfast; nobody photographs anyone asleep.
- **Films:** titles and ratings, never "a bit scary".
- **Private things:** bedwetting, sleepwalking or night fears go to the host alone.

### The child who wants to go home at 11 pm

Expect it. Almost all children, adolescents and adults feel some homesickness away from familiar people and places, says the [American Academy of Pediatrics report by Thurber and Walton (2007)](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/17200288); we read its abstract only.

- Move them to a quiet, lit room with a drink.
- Offer a choice: 20 minutes sitting with you, or a call home.
- If home wins, call the parent together on speaker.
- Tell the others "she has an early start".

Never bargain or tease. Leaving early should cost the child nothing socially.

### How much sleep is enough after a late night?

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine [consensus (Paruthi, 2016)](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC4877308) recommends 9 to 12 hours at ages 6 to 12 and 8 to 10 hours at 13 to 18. In a [2014 crossover experiment with 50 teens aged 14 to 17](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC4047523), five nights of 6.5 hours in bed left them more tense, angry, confused and fatigued, with poorer emotion regulation, than five nights of 10 hours. One night is not five, but teens often arrive short of sleep, so let them sleep until 9:30.

## The grown-up sleepover: friends, no kids, the same 8 slots

An adult sleepover runs the same timeline, 7:30 pm to 11 am. Guests pick their own scare level; four things change.

- **Beds first:** assign sleeping spots in the invitation, sofa included.
- **Split the shop:** one person buys; everyone pays their share next morning.
- **Drinks optional:** keep two alcohol-free options out.
- **Phones in a bowl for the story:** the 39-minute Benson tale needs darkness.

## A Halloween card for the friend who hosted

Our [Halloween greeting page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) is built for a single person. It won't send invitations or host a game; send it next morning to one friend, perhaps the host.

Bestie mode changes the final question to "Will you be my boo-st friend forever?". Before that, your friend lights a carved pumpkin, clears fog from portraits to reveal up to six photos, and reads your letter by torchlight in an attic.

They mix a potion from three to five memories you pick, like the joker card, and finish with a 1080×1920 Boo License. You're emailed when they first answer. Across the platform, pages average 11.1 recorded views.

For a child, Kids tone swaps in round blushing ghosts, and nothing goes dark. To have it open at pickup time, the [premium version](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) offers an unlock time and a voice note of up to 60 seconds.

## When a Halloween sleepover is the wrong plan: 3 cases

- **Under 8, or a first night away:** hold a "late-over" with pyjamas, a film and the Saki story, then collect at 9 pm.
- **A child with diagnosed anxiety or night fears:** their parent picks the story and film.
- **Everyone is together already:** a handwritten note in the pillowcase beats a link; our page is also English only.

## Sources

- [Recreational Fear Across Childhood](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40522538), 16 June 2025.
- [Sleep restriction worsens mood and emotion regulation in adolescents](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC4047523), 2014. Abstract read.
- [Preventing and treating homesickness](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/17200288), January 2007.
- [Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC4877308), 15 June 2016.
- [Beasts and Super-Beasts](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/269), 1914.
- [The Room in the Tower and Other Stories](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/72421), 1912.

sources.stat: Taranu, Clasen, Rosas, Dodd & Andersen, Child Psychiatry & Human Development (Springer; CC BY per Crossref licence record). Survey of 1,600 parents/caregivers of children aged 1-17 across 19 recreational-fear activity categories; 93% of children reported to enjoy at least one; distinct age-related trends. ABSTRACT ONLY read via the Europe PMC REST API: link.springer.com served a bot challenge, not worked around.

Baum, Desai, Field, Miller, Rausch & Beebe, J Child Psychol Psychiatry (2014 issue; online 30 July 2013). 50 adolescents aged 14-17, randomised crossover: 5 nights of 6.5 h in bed vs 5 nights of 10 h; during restriction teens rated themselves more tense/anxious, angry/hostile, confused and fatigued, with poorer emotion regulation per parents and teens. Abstract read via Europe PMC REST API (full-text endpoint returned 500).

Thurber & Walton for the AAP Council on School Health, Pediatrics 119(1):192-201. 'Almost all children, adolescents, and adults experience some degree of homesickness when they are apart from familiar people and environments.' Abstract only (publications.aap.org returned 403).

Paruthi et al., AASM consensus, J Clin Sleep Med. Children 6-12 years should sleep 9-12 hours per 24 hours; teenagers 13-18 should sleep 8-10 hours. Verified against AASM's own PDF (aasm.org/resources/pdf/pediatricsleepdurationconsensus.pdf); the PMC page is behind a bot check.

Saki, Beasts and Super-Beasts (transcribed from the 1914 John Lane edition), contains 'The Open Window': 1,208 words by plain count of the Gutenberg text; read-aloud time is our estimate at 150 wpm. Text read in full.

E. F. Benson, The Room in the Tower and Other Stories (Gutenberg header: original publication London, Mills & Boon, 1912), contains 'The Bus-Conductor' (3,462 words; hearse driver's 'Just room for one inside, sir', the bus conductor with the same face) and 'How Fear Departed from the Long Gallery' (5,892 words; ghost twins, ends with pity breaking the curse). Word counts by plain count of the Gutenberg text; read-aloud times are our 150 wpm estimate. Texts read.

structuralLimitations: The task prompt asked for 24–30 ideas; the post carries 25 (the draft had 27; two were cut to bring the body under the 1,800-word cap).
The prompt asked for a table with one row per timeline slot (8 rows); BRIEF §9 mandates 3–5 rows ALWAYS, so the 8 slots are grouped into 4 blocks.
No Halloween first-party data exists; the three facts are platform-wide (2026-09-24 vintage) and the post never implies Halloween usage.

Paruthi 2016 (AASM) was used once in b2 (family-halloween-movies); the prompt allowed one reuse and it is new to b4. Two alternatives were tried first: cdc.gov/sleep returned 403, and no other open-access paediatric duration consensus was found.

Taranu 2025, Thurber 2007 and Baum 2014 were read as abstracts only (Springer bot challenge, AAP 403, Europe PMC full-text 500); the body says so for Taranu and Thurber, and the Baum claim stays within its abstract.

No open-access paper on sleepovers and friendship exists in Europe PMC: an ABSTRACT/TITLE search for 'sleepover', 'sleepovers' and 'slumber party' returned 22 hits, none about children's friendships. The research slot is filled by the scary-activities route the prompt allowed (Taranu 2025, recreational fear in children).

Story clash found on the pre-finalise re-read of b4/blogs: halloween-games-for-seniors (written in parallel) reads Jacobs's 'The Monkey's Paw' aloud, so the draft's Jacobs picks were swapped for two E. F. Benson stories nobody in b1–b4 uses. halloween-ideas-for-teachers (also parallel, not a named sibling) uses Saki's 'The Open Window' as a 6–8 classroom inference lesson; it is kept here as the 8–12 lights-out read because no other short, gore-free public-domain ghost story unused in b1–b4 was found (Kwaidan appears in two movie posts, Riley's 'Little Orphant Annie' in halloween-quotes-for-kids, Twain's 'The Golden Arm' rejected for its racial-dialect framing). Orchestrator may swap it.
Story read-aloud times are the writer's estimate at 150 words a minute from plain word counts of the Gutenberg texts; Gutenberg is cap-exempt in verify.config.json.
SERP: 1 WebSearch (US index). Top 9 included 3 hijacked-subdomain spam copies (static.intrafocus.com x2, netbox.point-broadband.com); adobe.com returned 403 and was judged from its snippet only.
